claim: C. elegans Notch signaling maintains a pool of germline stem cells within their single-celled mesenchymal niche.
source: C. elegans Notch signaling maintains a pool of germline stem cells within their single-celled mesenchymal niche.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about the system being studied, supported by the experimental work presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: Notch-dependent active transcription sites occur in a probabilistic fashion in germline stem cells.
source: We find that Notch-dependent active transcription sites occur in a probabilistic fashion and, unexpectedly, do so in a steep gradient across the stem cell pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH data showing that not all nuclei have active transcription sites at any given time, and quantitative analysis of ATS distribution.

claim: Notch-dependent active transcription sites occur in a steep gradient across the stem cell pool.
source: We find that Notch-dependent active transcription sites occur in a probabilistic fashion and, unexpectedly, do so in a steep gradient across the stem cell pool.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis showing graded distribution of ATS from distal to proximal regions of the gonad.

claim: Graded nuclear active transcription sites create a nearly uniform field of mRNAs that extends beyond the region of transcriptional activation.
source: Yet these graded nuclear sites create a nearly uniform field of mRNAs that extends beyond the region of transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ATS distribution (Figure 3A) with mRNA distribution (Figure 3G,H) showing different spatial patterns.

claim: Active transcription sites provide a precise view of where the Notch-dependent transcriptional complex is productively engaged.
source: Therefore, active transcription sites provide a precise view of where the Notch-dependent transcriptional complex is productively engaged.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ATS represent nascent transcripts and are more spatially restricted than mRNAs.

claim: The Notch pathway is strongly conserved across animal phylogeny.
source: The Notch pathway is strongly conserved across animal phylogeny (e.g. Gazave et al. 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Notch is central to development and homeostasis, with dysfunction or misregulation causing disease.
source: Moreover, like other canonical signaling pathways, Notch is central to development and homeostasis, with dysfunction or misregulation causing disease (e.g. cancer, stroke) (Bray, 2006; Roy et al., 2007; Kopan and Ilagan, 2009; Tien et al., 2009; de la Pompa and Epstein, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The molecular mechanism of Notch signaling is essentially the same across metazoans, including nematodes, flies and vertebrates.
source: The molecular mechanism of Notch signaling is essentially the same across metazoans, including nematodes, flies and vertebrates.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Notch signaling conservation.

claim: Notch ligands trigger cleavage of the Notch receptor to release its intracellular domain (NICD), which assembles into a nuclear complex to activate transcription.
source: Briefly, Notch ligands trigger cleavage of the Notch receptor to release its intracellular domain (NICD), which assembles into a nuclear complex to activate transcription (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of Notch signaling supported by citation.

claim: No analyses of the Notch transcriptional response have been done at the resolution of nascent transcripts at active transcription sites in the nucleus.
source: The transcriptional response to Notch signaling has been analyzed in diverse systems (e.g. Shimojo et al., 2008; Ilagan et al. 2011; Hoyle and Ish-Horowicz, 2013; Imayoshi et al., 2013; Kershner et al., 2014; Jenkins et al., 2015), but no analyses have been done at the resolution of nascent transcripts at active transcription sites in the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is based on review of existing literature and establishes the novelty of the current work.

claim: Transcriptional reporters are both artificial and indirect readouts of the Notch transcriptional response.
source: Transcriptional reporters are a common readout of the Notch transcriptional response (Hansson et al., 2006; Imayoshi et al., 2013), but they are both artificial and indirect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of reporter constructs compared to endogenous gene expression.

claim: Conventional RNA in situ hybridization to endogenous Notch targets cannot resolve individual chromosomal loci and typically cannot resolve individual cells.
source: Conventional RNA in situ hybridization to endogenous Notch targets has also been used as a readout of Notch signaling, for example during segmentation of the zebrafish embryo (Hoyle and Ish-Horowicz, 2013), but this method cannot resolve individual chromosomal loci and typically cannot resolve individual cells.
evidence: This is based on known technical limitations of conventional in situ hybridization methods.

claim: GLP-1/Notch is crucial for the regulation of the germline stem cell pool and establishing polarity in the germline.
source: It had been known for some time that Notch, known as GLP-1/Notch in this system, is crucial for the regulation of the germline stem cell pool and establishing polarity in the germline (Austin and Kimble, 1987; Kimble and Crittenden, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The distal tip cell (DTC) uses Notch signaling to maintain a pool of germline stem cells (GSCs) at the distal end of the progenitor zone.
source: The single-celled mesenchymal niche, called the distal tip cell (DTC), uses Notch signaling to maintain a pool of germline stem cells (GSCs) at the distal end of the 'progenitor zone' in the distal gonad (Figure 1A,B) (Kimble and White 1981; Crittenden et al., 2006; Cinquin et al., 2010; Byrd et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The DTC cell body caps the distal gonad and extends ultra-thin processes intercalating throughout the GSC pool as well as long external processes along the entire progenitor zone and sometimes beyond.
source: The site of Notch signaling is ambiguous, because of the elaborate architecture of the signaling cell — the DTC cell body caps the distal gonad and extends ultra-thin processes intercalating throughout the GSC pool as well as long external processes along the entire progenitor zone and sometimes beyond (Fitzgerald and Greenwald, 1995; Hall et al., 1999; Crittenden et al., 2006; Byrd et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies of the DTC.

claim: sygl-1 and lst-1 are direct targets of GLP-1/Notch signaling and key regulators of germline stem cell maintenance.
source: In addition, two direct Notch target genes are available for assays: sygl-1 (synthetic Glp) and lst-1 (lateral signaling target) encode key stem cell regulators, whose removal mimics the loss of Notch signaling (Kershner et al., 2014) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The DTC expresses DSL ligands in both larvae and adults.
source: Thus, the DTC expresses DSL ligands in both larvae and adults (Henderson et al., 1994; Nadarajan et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous expression studies.

claim: Mitotically dividing germ cells express the GLP-1/Notch receptor at all stages.
source: mitotically dividing germ cells express the GLP-1/Notch receptor at all stages (Crittenden et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous expression studies.

claim: GLP-1/Notch signaling controls GSC maintenance throughout life of the animal.
source: and GLP-1/Notch signaling controls GSC maintenance throughout life of the animal (Austin and Kimble, 1987; Morgan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: sygl-1 exon probes detect both nascent transcripts in the nucleus and mature mRNAs in the cytoplasm.
source: The sygl-1 exon probes likely highlight Notch-dependent nascent transcripts in the nucleus as well as mature mRNAs in the cytoplasm, while intron probes likely mark only nascent nuclear transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing different localization patterns and confirmed by α-amanitin and RNAi experiments.

claim: sygl-1 intron probes mark only nascent nuclear transcripts.
source: The sygl-1 exon probes likely highlight Notch-dependent nascent transcripts in the nucleus as well as mature mRNAs in the cytoplasm, while intron probes likely mark only nascent nuclear transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that intron probes only detect nuclear spots and these are abolished by α-amanitin treatment.

claim: Treatment with α-amanitin abolished the nuclear dots for both exon and intron probes, but not the cytoplasmic dots.
source: First, treatment with α-amanitin, a standard RNA polymerase II inhibitor, abolished the nuclear dots for both exon and intron probes, but not the cytoplasmic dots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nuclear dots detected by smFISH are nascent transcripts and identify active transcription sites (ATS).
source: Therefore, nuclear dots are nascent transcripts and identify active transcription sites (ATS).
evidence: This is inferred from the α-amanitin experiment showing that nuclear dots are sensitive to RNA polymerase II inhibition.

claim: sygl-1 RNAi eliminated the cytoplasmic but not the nuclear dots seen with exon probes.
source: Second, sygl-1 RNAi eliminated the cytoplasmic but not the nuclear dots seen with exon probes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: RNAi depletes mature but not primary transcripts.
source: Because RNAi depletes mature but not primary transcripts (Maamar et al., 2013), the cytoplasmic dots must be mRNAs
evidence: This is based on cited knowledge about RNAi mechanism and used to interpret the experimental results.

claim: sygl-1 smFISH signals were not found in glp-1 null mutants.
source: Finally, we confirmed Notch dependence: sygl-1 smFISH signals were not found in glp-1 null mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Transcription from let-858, a non-target gene, was unaffected in glp-1 null mutants.
source: whereas transcription from a non-target gene, let-858, was unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D)
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D, serving as a negative control.

claim: sygl-1 smFISH signals expanded in a glp-1 gain-of-function mutant.
source: moreover, sygl-1 smFISH signals expanded in a glp-1 gain-of-function mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: The intensities of sygl-1 cytoplasmic mRNAs clustered tightly, corresponding to a single mRNA.
source: The intensities of the sygl-1 cytoplasmic mRNAs clustered tightly (Figure 2B), a nearly uniform signal that likely corresponds to a single mRNA (Raj et al., 2008; Raj and Tyagi, 2010; Lee et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2015; Padovan-Merhar et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B and supported by citations to previous work on single-molecule detection.

claim: sygl-1 ATS intensities spanned a broad range using either the exon or intron probe.
source: By contrast, sygl-1 ATS intensities spanned a broad range using either the exon (Figure 2C) or intron (Figure 2D) probe.
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Mean ATS intensity is roughly 17-fold greater on average than the mean single mRNA intensity.
source: Comparison of nuclear and cytoplasmic signal intensities, obtained with the same probe set (exon), revealed a mean ATS intensity roughly 17-fold greater on average than the mean single mRNA intensity (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is calculated from quantitative data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Roughly 17 nascent transcripts are generated at individual sygl-1 ATS, on average.
source: This 17-fold value suggests that roughly 17 nascent transcripts are generated at individual sygl-1 ATS, on average.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 17-fold intensity difference between ATS and single mRNA.

claim: The progenitor zone includes ~4% germ cells in G1, ~71% in S-phase, ~22% in G2 and ~3% in M-phase.
source: The progenitor zone includes ~4% germ cells in G1, ~71% in S-phase, ~22% in G2 and ~3% in M-phase (Seidel and Kimble, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous work characterizing cell cycle distribution.

claim: The maximum number of ATS per nucleus was four.
source: Indeed, the maximum number of ATS per nucleus was four (Figure 2E), as expected for the maximum number of sygl-1 chromosomal loci in this population of actively dividing cells.
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Individual sygl-1 loci within the same nucleus can be activated independently.
source: Indeed, most nuclei with any ATS had only one, while some had three (Figure 2E), demonstrating that individual sygl-1 loci within the same nucleus could be activated independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nuclei can have different numbers of ATS, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The intensities of ATS pairs within single nuclei failed to correlate with each other.
source: The intensities of ATS pairs failed to correlate with each other (Figure 2F), consistent with independent gene activation within the nucleus of a receiving cell.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F with Pearson correlation coefficient.

claim: Nuclear size is a good measure of cell cycle progression in 3-D reconstructed gonads.
source: We first confirmed in our 3-D reconstructed gonads that nuclear size was a good measure of cell cycle progression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), as previously established (Seidel and Kimble, 2015).
evidence: This is confirmed by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cell cycle stage is not linked to position along the gonadal axis in reconstructed gonads.
source: We also confirmed in the reconstructed gonads that cell cycle stage was not linked to position along the gonadal axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), also as previously established (Crittenden et al., 2006).
evidence: This is confirmed by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There is no significant difference in DNA content or nuclear size between cells with and without ATS.
source: We then assessed cells with and without ATS for both DNA content and nuclear size, but found no significant difference for either cell cycle measure (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: There is no correlation between summed ATS signal intensities per nucleus and either DNA content or nuclear size.
source: To ask if cell cycle stage might instead affect the full sygl-1 output per nucleus, we summed ATS signal intensities in each nucleus, but found no correlation between those summed values and either DNA content or nuclear size (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: The sporadic appearance of Notch-dependent ATS cannot be explained by a link with cell cycle stage.
source: We conclude that the sporadic appearance of Notch-dependent ATS cannot be explained by a link with cell cycle stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between ATS presence/intensity and cell cycle markers.

claim: The vast majority of sygl-1 ATS were restricted to a region of 1–30 µm (~1–7 gcd) from the distal end.
source: The vast majority of sygl-1 ATS were restricted to a region of 1–30 µm (~1–7 gcd) from the distal end (Figure 3A–F, dashed red line) and their distribution was graded within that region.
evidence: This is directly observed in the spatial distribution data shown in Figures 3A-F.

claim: The percentage of ATS-positive nuclei was graded from ~70% at the distal-most end to <5% at the proximal edge of the region with most ATS.
source: Thus, the percentage of ATS-positive nuclei was graded from ~70% at the distal-most end to <5% at the proximal edge of the region with most ATS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the quantitative data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability of ATS firing is graded within the distal third of the progenitor zone.
source: Therefore, the probability of ATS firing is graded within the distal third of the progenitor zone.
evidence: This is inferred from the graded percentage of ATS-positive nuclei shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The mean number of transcripts per ATS was not graded across the distal third of the progenitor zone.
source: Although ATS signal intensities varied considerably (Figure 3E), their mean was relatively constant across the distal third of the progenitor zone (Figure 3E, blue line). Therefore, unlike the steep gradient in probability of sygl-1 transcriptional activation, the mean number of transcripts per ATS was not graded.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ATS intensity as a function of position shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The mean of summed ATS intensities per nucleus was graded.
source: The mean of these summed intensities was graded (Figure 3F, blue line), consistent with the gradient in the number of sygl-1 ATS per nucleus (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: GLP-1/Notch signaling activates transcription in a graded fashion in the distal C. elegans gonad based on the probability of transcriptional activation.
source: We conclude that GLP-1/Notch signaling activates transcription in a graded fashion in the distal C. elegans gonad, and that this gradient reflects the probability of transcriptional activation, both in single cells (Figure 3A) and individual chromosomal loci (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple observations about graded ATS distribution and probability.

claim: sygl-1 ATS were not graded in glp-1(gf) germlines, but instead had an essentially uniform distribution.
source: The sygl-1 ATS were not graded in glp-1(gf) germlines, but instead had an essentially uniform distribution and were generated at a level similar to that of the wild-type far-distal gonad with respect to both ATS probability and intensity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The unregulated GLP-1/Notch receptor does not increase signaling activity per se but instead drives signaling ectopically.
source: Therefore, the unregulated GLP-1/Notch receptor does not increase signaling activity per se but instead drives signaling ectopically.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glp-1(gf) has uniform ATS distribution at wild-type intensity levels rather than increased intensity.

claim: Most sygl-1 mRNAs were restricted to a region of 1–45 µm (~1–10 gcd) from the distal end.
source: Most sygl-1 mRNAs were restricted to a region of 1–45 µm (~1–10 gcd) from the distal end (Figure 3G, dashed purple line).
evidence: This is directly observed in the spatial distribution data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Virtually all cells had sygl-1 mRNA in the distal-most region (1–20 µm or ~1–5 gcd), with the percentage decreasing more proximally.
source: Moreover, virtually all cells had sygl-1 mRNA in the distal-most region (1–20 µm or ~1–5 gcd), with the percentage decreasing more proximally (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The mRNA pattern was distinct from the ATS pattern.
source: Therefore, the mRNA pattern was distinct from the ATS pattern, even though both were assessed using the same exon probe and same images.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of Figures 3A and 3G,H showing different spatial distributions.

claim: sygl-1 nascent transcripts provide a more direct and accurate readout of GLP-1/Notch activated transcription than sygl-1 mRNA.
source: We conclude that sygl-1 nascent transcripts provide a more direct and accurate readout of GLP-1/Notch activated transcription than sygl-1 mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATS are more spatially restricted and directly reflect active transcription.

claim: Cells with many sygl-1 mRNAs can reside immediately adjacent to a neighbor with few or no sygl-1 mRNAs.
source: Instead, we asked if neighboring cells had similar mRNA densities and found cells with many sygl-1 mRNAs residing immediately adjacent to a neighbor with few or no sygl-1 mRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ATS-positive cells had more sygl-1 mRNAs than did ATS-negative cells, and both had more than the rachis in the distal-most gonad.
source: However, ATS-positive cells had more sygl-1 mRNAs than did ATS-negative cells, and both had more than the rachis in the distal-most gonad (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: DTC-germ cell contacts occurred in a gradient that extended far beyond the region with sygl-1 ATS.
source: DTC-germ cell contacts occurred in a gradient that extended far beyond the region with sygl-1 ATS (Figure 3J,L).
evidence: This is directly observed in data shown in Figures 3J and 3L.

claim: Virtually all germ cells were in DTC contact at the distal end, ~60% of germ cells remained in contact at 7 gcd from the distal end, and ~40% were still in contact more proximally at 13 gcd from the distal end.
source: Virtually all germ cells were in DTC contact at the distal end, ~60% of germ cells remained in contact at 7 gcd from the distal end, and ~40% were still in contact more proximally at 13 gcd from the distal end (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of DTC contact shown in Figure 3J.

claim: DTC contacts were much more extensive than the Notch-dependent ATS.
source: Therefore, DTC contacts were much more extensive than the Notch-dependent ATS.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of DTC contact distribution (Figure 3J) with ATS distribution (Figure 3K).

claim: The DTC was in contact with nearly all ATS-positive cells as well as with many ATS-negative cells.
source: Most importantly, the DTC was in contact with nearly all ATS-positive cells as well as with many ATS-negative cells (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: DTC contact is likely necessary for Notch-dependent transcriptional activation, but does not ensure Notch-dependent transcriptional activation at any given time.
source: We conclude that DTC contact is likely necessary for Notch-dependent transcriptional activation, but that it does not ensure Notch-dependent transcriptional activation at any given time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nearly all ATS-positive cells contact DTC, but many DTC-contacting cells lack ATS.

claim: lst-1 ATS were detected in only some germ cell nuclei at the distal end, whereas lst-1 mRNAs were in most of them.
source: To investigate Notch-regulated transcriptional activation of a second gene, we assayed lst-1 ATS and mRNAs (Figure 4A) and found essentially the same features seen with sygl-1: lst-1 ATS were detected in only some germ cell nuclei at the distal end, whereas lst-1 mRNAs were in most of them (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most lst-1 ATS-positive nuclei had only one ATS but some had two, three or even four.
source: most lst-1 ATS-positive nuclei had only one ATS but some had two, three or even four (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pairwise comparisons of lst-1 ATS intensities within a single nucleus revealed little correlation.
source: and pairwise comparisons of ATS intensities within a single nucleus revealed little correlation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Individual lst-1 genes are activated independently.
source: Therefore, like sygl-1, individual lst-1 genes are activated independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between lst-1 ATS intensities within the same nucleus.

claim: At any given time, GLP-1/Notch can activate transcription of sygl-1 only, lst-1 only, both loci or neither.
source: Therefore, at any given time, GLP-1/Notch can activate transcription of sygl-1 only, lst-1 only, both loci or neither.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nuclei can have different combinations of sygl-1 and lst-1 ATS (Figures 4G,H).

claim: Within a single nucleus, the numbers of sygl-1 and lst-1 ATS and their summed ATS intensities were not correlated.
source: Within a single nucleus, the numbers of sygl-1 and lst-1 ATS and their summed ATS intensities were not correlated (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: Notch activates transcription independently at individual chromosomal loci.
source: This finding with a second gene strongly supports the conclusion that Notch activates transcription independently at individual chromosomal loci.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between sygl-1 and lst-1 ATS within the same nucleus.

claim: GLP-1(q224) harbors a missense mutation that renders its NICD temperature sensitive for assembly into the Notch-dependent transcription complex.
source: Molecularly, GLP-1(q224) harbors a missense mutation that renders its NICD temperature sensitive for assembly into the Notch-dependent transcription complex (Figure 5A) (Kodoyianni et al., 1992; Petcherski and Kimble, 2000).
evidence: This is based on previous molecular characterization cited from the literature.

claim: The wild-type sygl-1 transcriptional response was indistinguishable in animals raised at 15, 20 and 25°C.
source: The wild-type sygl-1 transcriptional response was indistinguishable in animals raised at 15, 20 and 25°C (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: glp-1(q224) mutants raised at 15°C and shifted to 25°C as adults lost most sygl-1 ATS within 15 min after the shift.
source: By contrast, glp-1(q224) mutants raised at 15°C and shifted to 25°C as adults lost most sygl-1 ATS within 15 min after the shift (Figure 5B,C)
evidence: This is directly observed in the time course data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: sygl-1 mRNAs were lost more slowly but most were gone within three hours after temperature shift in glp-1(q224) mutants.
source: sygl-1 mRNAs were lost more slowly but most were gone within three hours (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the time course data shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: The half-life of GLP-1(q224)-dependent ATS is estimated to be <15 min.
source: From this data, we estimate the half-life of GLP-1(q224)-dependent ATS to be <15 min and sygl-1 mRNAs to be ~1 hr.
evidence: This is estimated from the kinetics of loss shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The half-life of sygl-1 mRNAs is estimated to be ~1 hr.
source: From this data, we estimate the half-life of GLP-1(q224)-dependent ATS to be <15 min and sygl-1 mRNAs to be ~1 hr.
evidence: This is estimated from the kinetics of loss shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: GLP-1(q224) is incapable of activating transcription in nematode germ cells at the restrictive temperature.
source: We conclude that GLP-1(q224) is incapable of activating transcription in nematode germ cells at the restrictive temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid loss of ATS after temperature shift to 25°C.

claim: glp-1(q224) progenitor zones are smaller than normal at 15°C.
source: Phenotypically, the GLP-1(q224) receptor appears weaker than the wild-type receptor at the permissive temperature: glp-1(q224) progenitor zones are smaller than normal at 15°C (Figure 6A) (Cinquin et al., 2010; Fox and Schedl, 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous phenotypic characterization cited from the literature and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The percentage of germ cell nuclei with sygl-1 ATS was about two-fold lower in glp-1(q224) mutants than in wild type.
source: The percentage of germ cell nuclei with sygl-1 ATS was about two-fold lower in glp-1(q224) mutants than in wild type (compare Figures 3A and 6B)
evidence: This is based on comparison of data shown in Figures 3A and 6B.

claim: Mean intensity of sygl-1 ATS was roughly two-fold lower in glp-1(q224) mutants than in wild type.
source: mean intensity of sygl-1 ATS was also roughly two-fold lower (compare Figures 3E and 6C, blue lines)
evidence: This is based on comparison of data shown in Figures 3E and 6C.

claim: Means of the summed intensities of sygl-1 ATS per nucleus were even more than two-fold lower in glp-1(q224) mutants than in wild type.
source: and means of the summed intensities of sygl-1 ATS per nucleus were even more than two-fold lower in the mutant (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the comparison shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The percentage of cells with sygl-1 mRNA was lower in glp-1(q224) mutants than in wild type.
source: In addition, the percentage of cells with sygl-1 mRNA was lower in glp-1(q224) mutants than in wild type (compare Figures 3G and 6E).
evidence: This is based on comparison of data shown in Figures 3G and 6E.

claim: mRNA number per cell was comparable to wild type in the distal-most cells of glp-1(q224) mutants.
source: Intriguingly, mRNA number per cell was comparable to wild type in the distal-most cells (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is based on comparison shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: NICD strength regulates both probability and intensity of transcriptional activation.
source: Because glp-1(q224) harbors a mutation in its NICD, we conclude that NICD strength regulates both probability and intensity of transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the q224 mutation affects both ATS probability and intensity.

claim: The sygl-1 ATS pattern was fully re-formed within an hour after reinstating signaling in glp-1(q224) mutants.
source: The answer was clear: the sygl-1 ATS pattern was fully re-formed within an hour. Both the percentage of nuclei with sygl-1 ATS and their spatial extent were the same as without any shift (Figure 7C, compare to Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the time course data shown in Figure 7C compared to Figure 6B.

claim: The mechanism underlying the spatially graded pattern of Notch-dependent ATS is not decay of the Notch response in germ cells as they move, but instead relies on the spatially graded Notch strength.
source: Therefore, the mechanism underlying the spatially graded pattern of Notch-dependent ATS is not decay of the Notch response in germ cells as they move, but instead relies on the spatially graded Notch strength (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid re-establishment of the ATS gradient, which is inconsistent with a decay model based on cell movement.

claim: Germline stem cells within their niche are subject to spatially modulated Notch signaling.
source: We conclude that germline stem cells within their niche are subject to spatially modulated Notch signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the graded pattern of ATS and the mechanism by which it is established.

claim: This work reports a high resolution and quantitative view of Notch-regulated transcriptional activation at endogenous genes in their natural context, a first for any canonical signaling pathway.
source: This work reports a high resolution and quantitative view of Notch-regulated transcriptional activation at endogenous genes in their natural context, a first for any canonical signaling pathway to our knowledge.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty of the work based on the methods and findings presented.

claim: Notch does not orchestrate a synchronous nuclear response but instead tunes the probability of transcriptional firing and number of nascent transcripts produced.
source: We find that Notch does not orchestrate a synchronous nuclear response but instead tunes the probability of transcriptional firing and number of nascent transcripts produced.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings showing probabilistic ATS firing and variable ATS intensities.

claim: Notch activates transcription independently at individual chromosomal loci.
source: Consistent with that conclusion, Notch activates transcription independently at individual chromosomal loci.
evidence: This is supported by lack of correlation between ATS intensities at different loci within the same nucleus.

claim: The pattern of nuclear active transcription sites (ATS) is not essentially the same as the pattern of cytoplasmic mRNAs.
source: We also overturn expectations that the pattern of nuclear active transcription sites (ATS) is essentially the same as the pattern of cytoplasmic mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of ATS and mRNA spatial distributions showing different patterns.

claim: ATS are generated in a steep probability gradient across the stem cell pool, but mRNAs are more uniform in the same region and extend beyond it.
source: ATS are generated in a steep probability gradient across the stem cell pool, but mRNAs are more uniform in the same region and extend beyond it.
evidence: This is based on comparison of spatial distributions shown in Figures 3A and 3G,H.

claim: NICD strength determines both probability of transcriptional firing and number of nascent transcripts per ATS.
source: We also find that NICD strength determines both probability of transcriptional firing and number of nascent transcripts per ATS, providing a new metric for Notch strength.
evidence: This is based on comparison of wild-type and glp-1(q224) mutant ATS patterns.

claim: Transcriptional bursting has emerged as a general phenomenon in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
source: Transcriptional bursting has emerged as a general phenomenon in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (e.g. Elowitz et al., 2002; Chubb et al., 2006; Raj et al., 2006; Boettiger and Levine, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: cAMP modulates transcriptional burst frequency in Dictyostelium.
source: Thus, cAMP modulates transcriptional burst frequency in Dictyostelium (Corrigan and Chubb, 2014)
evidence: This is cited from previous work on signaling-regulated transcription.

claim: MAPK modulates transcriptional burst frequency in tissue culture cells.
source: and MAPK modulates transcriptional burst frequency in tissue culture cells (Senecal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous work on signaling-regulated transcription.

claim: The sporadic appearance of Notch-responsive ATS is best explained by transcriptional 'bursts' or 'pulses' separated by periods of quiescence.
source: We suggest that the sporadic appearance of Notch-responsive ATS is best explained by transcriptional 'bursts' or 'pulses' separated by periods of quiescence (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the probabilistic ATS pattern based on known transcriptional bursting phenomena.

claim: Notch regulates the probability of transcription firing at endogenous genes in a wild-type intact tissue.
source: Regardless, our results show that Notch regulates the probability of transcription firing at endogenous genes in a wild-type intact tissue, which provides a critical foundation for future investigations with live imaging, which is expected to have lower resolution and typically relies on manipulated reporters.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings emphasizing their significance for future work.

claim: The mutant NICD is less capable than wild-type of forming or maintaining the Notch transcription complex in germ cells.
source: The simplest interpretation is that the mutant NICD is less capable than wild-type of forming or maintaining the Notch transcription complex in germ cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced transcriptional response in glp-1(q224) mutants at the permissive temperature.

claim: The molecular consequence of the mutant's two-fold lower transcriptional response is the generation of a shorter than normal ATS gradient.
source: The molecular consequence of the mutant's two-fold lower transcriptional response is the generation of a shorter than normal ATS gradient (this work)
evidence: This is directly observed in the data comparing wild-type and glp-1(q224) ATS distributions.

claim: The biological consequence of the mutant's two-fold lower transcriptional response is a reduced progenitor zone.
source: and its biological consequence is a reduced progenitor zone (Cinquin et al., 2010; Fox and Schedl, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous phenotypic characterization of glp-1(q224) mutants.

claim: NICD strength is important for fine-tuning the Notch response, with implications for pattern formation and disease.
source: The discovery that NICD strength modulates both probability and intensity of the Notch transcriptional response underscores the importance of the NICD for fine-tuning the Notch response, with implications for pattern formation and disease.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings regarding their broader significance.

claim: A high-resolution ATS assay is powerful for assessing molecular consequences of any condition that affects Notch transcriptional activation.
source: This finding also highlights the power of a high-resolution ATS assay for assessing molecular consequences of any condition (e.g. defects in any component in the pathway as well as physiological or environmental factors) that affect Notch transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of the method based on its ability to detect differences in NICD strength.

claim: GLP-1/Notch signaling from the DTC niche maintains a pool of germline stem cells and establishes polarity and patterning in the germline tissue.
source: GLP-1/Notch signaling from the DTC niche not only maintains a pool of germline stem cells but also establishes polarity and patterning in the germline tissue (Kimble and White 1981; Austin and Kimble, 1987; Lander et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GLP-1/Notch activates transcription over a defined region (7 germ cell diameters from the distal end) and its nuclear response is steeply graded over that region.
source: We now learn that GLP-1/Notch activates transcription over a defined region (7 germ cell diameters from the distal end) and that its nuclear response is steeply graded over that region.
evidence: This is based on the spatial distribution data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GLP-1/Notch forms a gradient of ATS probability rather than ATS size.
source: Importantly, GLP-1/Notch forms a gradient of ATS probability rather than ATS size, and to our knowledge, no gradient of this type has been seen before.
evidence: This is based on the observation that ATS probability is graded but mean ATS intensity is not.

claim: Graded loss of active transcription sites at loci encoding key stem cell regulators is likely the molecular basis of the 'initial trigger' for stem cells to begin their transition towards a differentiated state.
source: Regardless, we suggest that graded loss of active transcription sites at loci encoding key stem cell regulators is likely the molecular basis of the long sought 'initial trigger' for stem cells to begin their transition towards a differentiated state and, as such, this gradient is likely to be critical for establishing size of the stem cell pool.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the ATS gradient.

claim: Cytoplasmic mRNAs provide a commonly used readout of the Notch transcriptional response.
source: Cytoplasmic mRNAs provide a commonly used readout of the Notch transcriptional response and clearly their distribution is crucial biologically.
evidence: This is general knowledge about common experimental approaches.

claim: Notch-dependent mRNAs generate two key stem cell regulators, SYGL-1 and LST-1, that maintain a pool of stem cells with apparently equivalent developmental potential.
source: In the C. elegans distal gonad for example, Notch-dependent mRNAs generate two key stem cell regulators, SYGL-1 and LST-1, that maintain a pool of stem cells with apparently equivalent developmental potential (Kershner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous functional characterization.

claim: The distributions of Notch-dependent ATS and mRNAs are not the same.
source: Yet the distributions of Notch-dependent ATS and mRNAs are not the same.
evidence: This is based on comparison of spatial distributions shown in Figures 3A and 3G,H.

claim: At any given position, more germ cells had sygl-1 and lst-1 mRNAs than had sygl-1 and lst-1 ATS.
source: At any given position, more germ cells had sygl-1 and lst-1 mRNAs than had sygl-1 and lst-1 ATS, and mRNAs extended more proximally than ATS (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of ATS and mRNA distributions shown in multiple figures.

claim: Notch-dependent ATS may be less stable than Notch-dependent mRNAs.
source: One simple explanation for the ATS vs. mRNA difference is that Notch-dependent ATS may be less stable than Notch-dependent mRNAs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences in ATS and mRNA distributions.

claim: Notch-dependent ATS are a more accurate assay of Notch activity than mRNAs.
source: Therefore, Notch-dependent ATS are a more accurate assay of Notch activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the shorter half-life of ATS compared to mRNAs and their more restricted spatial distribution.

claim: Notch-dependent ATS reveal transcriptional activation, the ultimate test of productive Notch signaling.
source: We note however that Notch-dependent ATS reveal transcriptional activation, the ultimate test of productive Notch signaling, and that ATS also provide a quantitative readout of signaling strength.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of using ATS as a readout.

claim: ATS provide a quantitative readout of signaling strength.
source: We note however that Notch-dependent ATS reveal transcriptional activation, the ultimate test of productive Notch signaling, and that ATS also provide a quantitative readout of signaling strength.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ability to detect differences between wild-type and mutant NICD.

claim: The C. elegans gonad was uniquely suited for this analysis because of its defined signaling cell and continuous activity across a field of many receiving cells.
source: The C. elegans gonad was uniquely suited for this analysis because of its defined signaling cell and continuous activity across a field of many receiving cells, which offered statistical power for quantitating the probabilistic nuclear response.
evidence: This is an inference about why this system was particularly suitable for the study.

claim: All canonical signaling pathways will likely follow guidelines similar to those found here for Notch.
source: We suspect that all canonical signaling pathways will follow guidelines similar to those found here for Notch.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation of the findings to other signaling pathways.

claim: Assaying nascent transcripts at active transcription sites is the most accurate readout for canonical signaling.
source: Our findings offer a new window into the Notch transcriptional response and demonstrate the importance of assaying nascent transcripts at active transcription sites as the most accurate readout for canonical signaling.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings emphasizing the methodological contribution.
